A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, and the methods, equations, tables, figures, and retained studies can be matched reliably across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, user studies, expert validation, and verifier-robustness experiments, including Tables 1–2 and 9–16.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds MMMU-Pro results, generated-distractor experiments, a model-confidence comparison, and a VizWiz error audit.

M1.justification: v2 adds a GPT-4o candidate-generation step using the image, question, and ground-truth answers to enable Contrastiveness scoring on open-ended VizWiz answers (Appendix F). v1 explicitly omitted this evaluation after unsuccessful negative mining. This extends the scoring procedure, while the VF and Contrastiveness algorithms and combination formulas remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMMU-Pro, extending evaluation to complex multidisciplinary visual reasoning beyond the retained A-OKVQA commonsense and VizWiz assistive-question domains. This substantially broadens task coverage. The human studies still use A-OKVQA and VizWiz.

E2.justification: Appendix H and Table 12 add a first-answer-token softmax confidence baseline for LLaVA-v1.5-7B on A-OKVQA and MMMU-Pro. The existing Simulatability, Informativeness, and Commonsense Plausibility comparators and human-study controls are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include evaluating 500 single-image MMMU-Pro examples with ten options and explanation-before-answer prompting, generating three distractors for post-hoc VizWiz scoring, reconstructing A-OKVQA candidate sets, and auditing incorrect predictions with VF above 0.9. These are additions to the evaluation design; the retained human-study protocols do not establish any rerun or setting change.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds an original-versus-generated distractor ablation and semantic-similarity analysis. Appendix I adds VizWiz error cases and an expert audit reporting 20 selected cases per model. The verifier swaps, expert-agreement checks, presentation ablations, and three-stage user study already appeared in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use unpaired t-tests for Discriminability, bootstrap significance tests and standard-deviation reporting for user studies, and Cohen's kappa for expert agreement. Added comparisons reuse these practices; no changed seed counts, repeated-run counts, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add MMMU-Pro and previously absent VizWiz Contrastiveness/combination results; new appendix results cover distractor reconstruction, confidence baselines, and error analysis. For example, VizWiz GPT-4o Contrastiveness has Discriminability −0.097. A retained value also changes: A-OKVQA/LLaVA VF ECE is 0.207 in v1 Table 2 versus 0.197 in v2 Table 2, although v2 Tables 16 and 19 retain 0.207. Human-study numerical outcomes and uncertainties are unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of VF, Contrastiveness, their average/product/minimum combinations, and Discriminability are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added empirical procedures introduce no substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the claimed calibration and discrimination benefits to MMMU-Pro. The central contributions—two complementary explanation scores and improved user reliance—remain, including the same 11.1-percentage-point accuracy gain and 15.4-point reduction in falsely accepting incorrect predictions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking weak VizWiz discrimination to ground-truth mismatches, generated-distractor degradation to semantic proximity, and confidence-baseline effectiveness to task difficulty. Its limitations replace the closed-set restriction with dependence on distractor quality and add substantive concerns about demographic generalization and overreliance on quality scores.

D1.justification: v2 adds the MMMU-Pro and hard-negative prompts, specifies the similarity encoder and confidence-baseline implementation, and explicitly documents direct use of Vera. It also adds consent, review, screening, and licensing disclosures. These improve documentation; the code-access information and reported hardware and costs remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations concerning MMMU-Pro, verbalized calibration, distractor generation, helpful explanations, and selective explanation presentation. It distinguishes explanation-derived signals from verbalized confidence and acknowledges evidence that explanations can help detect errors. The existing research positioning is largely retained.

P1.justification: Most methodological and user-study prose is retained, with localized rewriting. Related Work moves to Appendix A, baseline definitions and detailed study procedures move into appendices, RQ2b is nested under RQ2, and limitations and ethics receive standalone sections. These are targeted structural and language revisions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts two-column formatting and extensively rebuilds the displays: Tables 1–2 gain benchmark and average columns, new analytical tables are added, calibration panels are rearranged, and user-study charts receive revised axes and labels. Figure 4's accuracy axis now begins at 0.50 instead of zero. v1 Table 13 is also split into v2 Tables 19–20.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a model-confidence comparison; v2 Table 12 usefully shows that LLaVA logits calibrate best on A-OKVQA while the combined explanation score performs better on MMMU-Pro. The broader evaluation and diagnostic analyses improve understanding of applicability. Gains are tempered by questionable distractor validity, including overlapping room/living room alternatives in Table 11, and unreconciled ECE values between Table 2 and the appendices. Overall, the added diagnostic evidence provides a limited net improvement.
